howItWorks.intro: The estimate is built from five inputs you control directly — restaurant meal frequency, your primary cooking oil at home, packaged food servings, fried or snack food frequency, and dressing or sauce use — each mapped to a typical seed oil content per occurrence, based on how much oil these food categories realistically contain per serving.
rules: Restaurant meals: most restaurants cook with soybean or canola oil — estimated 2-4 tbsp seed oil per meal
Cooking oil: home cooking with seed oils adds ~1-2 tbsp per meal; olive oil, butter, and coconut oil contain minimal linoleic acid
Packaged foods: most contain soybean, canola, or sunflower oil — ~0.5-1 tbsp seed oil per serving
Fried/snack foods: chips, fries, and fried foods are major sources — 1-3 tbsp per serving
Dressings and sauces: most commercial dressings are soybean oil-based — ~0.5-1 tbsp per serving
Linoleic acid: the primary omega-6 fatty acid in seed oils, making up 50-60% of soybean and corn oil
howItWorks.outro: For context, USDA food availability data puts average added fat and oil intake in the range of 40-80g per day for a typical U.S. eating pattern, and soybean oil alone accounts for a large share of that because it's the default frying and food-manufacturing oil. If your result lands well above that range, restaurant meals and packaged snacks are almost always the biggest levers — a single fried appetizer or bag of chips can add more seed oil than an entire day of home-cooked meals made with olive oil or butter.

faq.question: What counts as a seed oil?
faq.answer: Seed oils are vegetable oils extracted from the seeds of plants rather than fruit flesh or animal fat — soybean, corn, canola (rapeseed), sunflower, safflower, cottonseed, and grapeseed oil are the ones most common in US and UK food. They're mechanically pressed and typically solvent-extracted and refined, and they're high in polyunsaturated fat, mostly linoleic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid the body needs but cannot produce on its own.

faq.question: Where does most seed oil in a typical diet come from?
faq.answer: Overwhelmingly from three places: restaurant and takeout cooking (frying, sautéing, deep-frying), packaged and processed food (crackers, cookies, granola bars, most sliced bread), and condiments — bottled salad dressing, mayonnaise, and many sauces are built on a soybean or canola oil base. Home cooking with a bottle of "vegetable oil" is a source too, but for most people it's smaller than the restaurant and packaged-food totals combined.

faq.question: How do I estimate grams of seed oil from a nutrition label?
faq.answer: Check the total fat and the ingredient list. If soybean, canola, or sunflower oil is the primary fat source and it's listed near the top of the ingredients, most of the listed fat grams for that serving are a reasonable proxy for seed oil grams — a serving of crackers with 6g of fat and "soybean oil" as the second ingredient is close to 6g of seed oil per serving. Multiply by however many servings you actually eat, since package serving sizes are often smaller than a real portion. For a worked example: fast food fries cooked in a soybean-canola blend contribute roughly 15-20g of oil, a tablespoon of ranch dressing adds about 10g (mostly soybean oil), and a small bag of chips contributes another 6-8g — three items that together already put you at 30-38g of seed oil for the day.

faq.question: Is a high omega-6:omega-3 ratio actually harmful?
faq.answer: This is the genuinely contested part of the topic. Modern diets heavy in seed oils commonly run 10:1 to 20:1 (omega-6 to omega-3), compared with roughly 1:1 to 4:1 in diets built around less processed food. Some researchers argue this shift promotes chronic low-grade inflammation; other reviews find that typical dietary linoleic acid intake doesn't raise inflammatory markers in humans the way some animal or cell studies suggested, and note that linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid the diet needs some amount of. Mainstream nutrition guidance doesn't currently support the strongest harm claims circulating online, but the ratio — and how much it matters at ordinary intake levels — is an active area of research rather than settled fact.

faq.question: Should I try to eliminate seed oils completely?
faq.answer: That's a personal decision this calculator isn't positioned to make for you. If you're eating a varied diet with reasonable amounts of omega-3s (fatty fish, walnuts, flax, or chia), moderate seed oil intake from home cooking isn't something current mainstream nutrition guidance flags as a specific risk on its own. If you eat fried and packaged food often, this tool can at least show you where the bulk of your intake is actually coming from, so any change you make targets the biggest contributor rather than the smallest one.

faq.question: What oils are NOT seed oils, and are they automatically better?
faq.answer: Olive oil, avocado oil, coconut oil, butter, ghee, tallow, lard, and palm oil are fruit oils, animal fats, or tropical oils with different fatty acid profiles — generally lower in linoleic acid, though coconut oil and butter bring their own high saturated fat content, which carries its own separate considerations. "Not a seed oil" isn't automatically synonymous with healthier; it just means a different fat profile, and the right choice depends on your overall diet, not any single ingredient.

faq.question: Is this medical or dietary advice?
faq.answer: No. This is an educational estimate based on typical food-category values, not a personalized nutrition assessment. If you have a specific health concern, a diagnosed condition, or want tailored guidance on fat intake, talk to a registered dietitian or physician — they can account for your full diet and health history in a way a calculator can't.

howWeCalculate.intro: Each input maps to a gram-per-occurrence range drawn from typical nutrition-label and food-service serving data for the category it represents, rather than a single fixed multiplier — restaurant meals and fried foods sit at the high end because deep-frying and pan-searing use noticeably more oil than a packaged snack or a spoonful of dressing.
steps: Restaurant and takeout meals are weighted heaviest, since most kitchens fry and sauté with soybean or canola oil in volumes of roughly 2-4 tablespoons per meal

Your home cooking oil selection either adds to the total (vegetable, canola, or soybean oil) or contributes close to zero linoleic acid (olive oil, butter, ghee, coconut oil, avocado oil), reflecting the very different fatty acid profiles of these oils

Packaged food servings, fried/snack frequency, and dressing or sauce use are each converted to a weekly total and averaged into a daily gram estimate, using the same per-serving ranges shown in the food comparison table on this page

The combined daily oil figure is converted to grams of linoleic acid (using seed oils' typical 50-60% linoleic acid content), annualized, converted to calories at 9 calories per gram of fat, and used to estimate an omega-6:omega-3 ratio against a typical dietary omega-3 baseline
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are estimates built from typical food-category values, not a measurement of what you personally ate — restaurant recipes, brand formulations, and portion sizes vary. For a precise picture or personalized guidance, a registered dietitian can review your actual diet.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator is useful anywhere you want a realistic number instead of a guess about how much seed oil is actually in your diet.
scenarios: You've heard claims about seed oils online and want a realistic estimate of your own intake before deciding whether — or how much — to change anything
You're switching your primary home cooking oil (say, from vegetable oil to olive oil or avocado oil) and want to see how much that alone shifts your daily total
You eat out or order takeout often and want to see how much restaurant cooking oil contributes compared to what you cook at home
You're preparing questions for a registered dietitian or physician about your fat intake and want concrete numbers to bring to the conversation
You're curious how a diet heavy in packaged snacks and dressings compares, gram for gram, to a diet built around whole foods

sections.title: What the Seed Oil Intake Calculator Measures
sections.body: Seed oils are the vegetable oils pressed from oilseeds — soybean, corn, canola (rapeseed), sunflower, safflower, cottonseed, and grapeseed oil are the ones that show up most often in a US or UK kitchen. This calculator turns five everyday habits — how often you eat restaurant or takeout food, which oil you reach for at home, how many packaged or processed items you eat, how often you eat fried or salty snack foods, and how often you use dressings, mayo, or sauces — into a daily estimate: grams of seed oil, grams of linoleic acid (the specific omega-6 fat that dominates these oils), an annualized total, calories contributed by that oil, and an estimated omega-6:omega-3 ratio. It's built from typical serving-size and oil-content figures for common foods, not a metabolic test, so treat the output as a reasonable estimate of your pattern rather than a lab measurement.

sections.title: Why Seed Oil Intake Is Easy to Underestimate
sections.body: Most people who don't cook exclusively with olive oil or butter have no real sense of how much seed oil they eat, because it rarely appears as a standalone item on a plate — it's the medium other food is cooked in, or the base of a sauce. Consider a fairly ordinary lunch: fast food fries cooked in a soybean-canola blend contribute somewhere around 15-20g of oil, a tablespoon of ranch dressing adds roughly 10g (mostly soybean oil), and a small bag of chips contributes another 6-8g. That's already 30-38g of seed oil from three items, before counting the bread on a sandwich, the mayo in a wrap, or whatever oil a restaurant used to sauté dinner. A pattern like that repeated across a week adds up quickly — which is exactly the blind spot this calculator is meant to fill in.

sections.title: Reading the Omega-6 Ratio and What the Numbers Don't Tell You
sections.body: The tool also estimates an omega-6:omega-3 ratio, because that ratio — not seed oil intake in isolation — is the part of this topic that's genuinely debated in nutrition research. Some researchers argue a high ratio, common in diets that lean heavily on soybean and corn oil, promotes low-grade inflammation; others point out that the evidence linking typical dietary linoleic acid intake to those outcomes in humans is considerably weaker than online discussion suggests, and that linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid the body cannot make on its own. Both things can be true at once: seed oils are a real source of concentrated polyunsaturated fat, and the strongest claims of harm circulating online outrun what controlled human studies currently show. This calculator gives you a number to start from — it isn't medical or dietary advice, and a registered dietitian or physician is the right resource if you're changing your diet for a specific health reason.

howToSteps.title: Log Your Restaurant and Takeout Frequency
howToSteps.description: Start with restaurant/takeout meals per week — this single input carries the most weight, since most restaurants cook with soybean or canola oil in larger volumes than home cooking typically does.

howToSteps.title: Add Your Home Cooking and Packaged Food Habits
howToSteps.description: Select your primary cooking oil at home, then fill in packaged/processed food servings per day, fried/snack food frequency, and salad dressing/mayo/sauce usage — each one adds its own typical gram range to the total.

howToSteps.title: Calculate Your Estimate
howToSteps.description: Click "Estimate Seed Oil Intake" to run the numbers through the calculator's weighted per-category ranges.

howToSteps.title: Review Daily, Annual, and Ratio Results
howToSteps.description: Check est. daily seed oil, est. daily linoleic acid, annual seed oil, calories from seed oil, and the estimated omega-6:omega-3 ratio together — the ratio and the gram total tell different parts of the story, so it's worth looking at both.

tips: Check ingredient labels for "soybean oil," "canola oil," "vegetable oil," "corn oil," or "sunflower oil" near the top of the list — that's the fastest way to sanity-check your packaged food inputs.
Restaurant and fried food inputs move the total more than any other field, since a single fried item can contain more oil than a whole day of olive-oil home cooking.
If you don't know what oil a restaurant uses, assume soybean or canola — it's the default in most commercial fryers and sauté stations in the US.

The omega-6:omega-3 ratio matters more in context than the seed oil gram total alone — pairing seed-oil-heavy meals with fatty fish, walnuts, or flaxseed shifts the ratio even when total oil intake stays the same.
Re-run the calculator after a diet change — a new cooking oil, fewer takeout meals — to see the actual size of the shift rather than assuming.
